chat.author: Muhammad Usama Sardar
chat.text:
My point was: In ProVerif, tables are private by default. Maybe the protocol has something specific which I do not understand. 
I previously wanted to ask about how you specify anonymity vs. unlinkability in ProVerif.

chat.author: Vaishnavi Sundararajan
chat.text: When I say that tables are public, I do not mean that the adversary can look up stuff, but that they can see the result of looking stuff up, unlike, say, the use of private channels

chat.author: Vaishnavi Sundararajan
chat.text: For anonymity, we consider something like I (diff[skI1, skI2), ...) | R(skR, ...). For unlinkability, we consider I(diff[skI1, skI2), ...) | R(skR, ...) | I(skI1, ...). This is similar to how it is done for the PSK analysis as well. Essentially unlinkability is a much stronger property, saying that even if the adversary can see the interaction of a specific party with a specific other party, he cannot identify whether this same party is the one interacting in another execution. Does that help?

chat.author: Vaishnavi Sundararajan
chat.text:
Jonathan Hoyland said:

Vaishnavi Sundararajan Interesting, does that unlinkability property make sense in the real world? If I see two handshakes coming from the same device (which I can as a DY attacker) I can easily distinguish that from two handshakes coming from different devices.

Essentially the DY attacker only controls the network, so it's not necessary that they can see which device the handshake comes from (imagine there are switches/links in between the "originating" device and the channel -- as for exactly how realistic this is for LAKE, I cannot speak to). In general, what we are saying is that we would like it to be the case that even two different handshakes from the same device have enough freshness and encryption built into them that it is impossible to link them together to originating from the same device.
